Aadhya and Tatsuya connected three months ago through Tandem, a language exchange app, when Aadhya's attempt to learn Japanese through podcasts wasn't producing the conversational practice she needed. She'd matched with a handful of users before Tatsuya—his profile mentioned engineering and a preference for text-based practice, which suited her own measured communication style. Their first conversation had been awkward, full of the stilted pleasantries that characterize exchanges between people who genuinely want to connect but aren't sure how to bridge the distance. But Tatsuya's earnestness—his careful, over-edited messages, his habit of apologizing for his English even when it was perfectly correct—reminded Aadhya of something familiar. She recognized the particular kind of anxiety that makes someone revise a text five times before sending, the weight of wanting to get it right.

Over the weeks, they developed a routine: twice-weekly sessions where they alternated between English and Japanese practice, sharing fragments of their lives in the process. Aadhya learned that Tatsuya lived alone in Fukuoka, that he sent thumbs-up stickers to his mother because he didn't know what else to say, that he was studying engineering partly because he couldn't imagine what else to do. Tatsuya learned that Aadhya's parents sent her kurtis she hadn't asked for, that her closest friend had moved to Singapore, that she was good at her job without being certain she wanted it. They'd never video-called—both seemed to prefer the careful remove of text—and their profile photos remained the only images they had of each other.

Tonight's session was scheduled at Tatsuya's request. He has an English interview next week for a summer research program at a university in Singapore—the first real opportunity he's had to study abroad, and the first time his academic path has offered something he actually wants rather than something he should want. He's practiced his introduction a hundred times in front of his mirror, but the words feel different in his head than they do typed into the chat. Aadhya is on her balcony after work, the tulsi plant finally watered, her cousin Priya inside watching something on television. The day was unremarkable—the usual meetings, the usual commute, the usual feeling of doing fine—but something about Tatsuya's request feels like it matters. She wants to help him get this right.

They communicate in English, which Tatsuya is working to improve, with occasional Japanese phrases when Aadhya practices her vocabulary. She's still at the level where she can read hiragana slowly and recognize a handful of kanji, nowhere near conversational, but Tatsuya's patience with her questions about grammar has become one of the small reliable good things in her week.

He hasn't yet looked at the full requirements document, planning to "get the vibe" from conversation first. They're both aware this is a professional relationship with weight on both sides—Aditya needs to demonstrate competence to his supervisor and feels the pressure of institutional representation; Vivaan needs this project to go smoothly to prove his bandwidth after missing deadlines on another account last month.
